decks.title: Human Evolution — Part 1: Our ancestors
goals: Arrange the human ancestors from Australopithecus to modern man in sequence
Compare them in posture, cranial capacity, canines, brow ridges, chin, body hair and height
Identify a human ancestor from a description of its features

slides.heading: Human Evolution
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the members of the human line and how their bodies changed.

visual.alt: Flow of the human line: Australopithecus, Homo habilis, Homo erectus, Neanderthal man, Cro-Magnon man, modern man

slides.narration: Fossils of skulls, teeth and bones tell the story of our family tree. In this part we meet six members of the human line, from small brained Australopithecus to modern humans, and trace how the body and brain changed along the way.

slides.heading: The members of the human line

rows: Walked on two legs; small brain
Large brain; heavy brow ridges; buried the dead
Tall; chin; cave paintings; fine tools

visual.alt: Table of six members of the human line and what each is known for

slides.narration: Learn each member by one key idea. Australopithecus walked upright. Homo habilis made the first tools. Homo erectus used fire. Neanderthals buried their dead. Cro Magnon people painted caves. And modern humans built farms and cities.

slides.heading: Skulls compared
slides.body_md: Early skulls: **low braincase**, **sloping forehead**, **heavy brow ridges**, **projecting jaws**, **large canines**, **no chin**. Modern skull: **high, rounded braincase**, **steep forehead**, **small brow ridges**, **flat face**, **chin**.

slides.narration: Put the two skulls side by side. The early skull has a low braincase, a heavy ridge over the eyes and jaws that jut forward with no chin. The modern skull is tall and rounded, with a flat face and a clear chin.

slides.heading: Quick check: a modern feature
slides.body_md: Which feature is present in modern humans but absent in Australopithecus?
slides.narration: Look at the front of the lower jaw.

slides.heading: Bigger brains
slides.body_md: Approximate cranial capacity rose from about **500** cubic centimetres in Australopithecus to about **1600** in Cro-Magnon man; modern humans average about **1400**.

slides.narration: Cranial capacity is the volume of the braincase. It almost trebled along the human line. Notice that Neanderthal and Cro Magnon brains were as large as ours or larger, so brain size alone does not explain everything about modern humans.

slides.heading: Comparing the ancestors

rows: Partly stooped; walked on two legs
Short (about a metre and a half or less)

visual.alt: Table comparing early ancestors and modern humans in seven features

slides.narration: Seven features change in a clear direction. Posture becomes fully upright. The brain grows. Canines, brow ridges and body hair shrink. A chin appears. And height increases.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: name the fossil
slides.body_md: A skull has no chin, heavy brow ridges and a braincase of about 1000 cubic centimetres; the leg bones show a fully upright stance.
bullets: Step 1: **no chin** rules out Cro-Magnon and modern man.
Step 2: about **1000** is larger than Australopithecus (500) and Homo habilis (700) but smaller than Neanderthal man (1450).
Step 3: fully upright: **Homo erectus**.

visual.alt: Worked table: each clue and the ancestors it rules out, leaving Homo erectus

slides.narration: Use the clues to cross names off the list. No chin removes the two most recent forms. A braincase of about a thousand cubic centimetres removes the smallest and the largest. What is left is Homo erectus.

slides.heading: Quick check: the handy man
slides.body_md: Fill in: Homo habilis is known as the ______ man.
slides.narration: It made the first stone tools.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: how much bigger?
slides.body_md: Compare the braincase of Australopithecus with ours.
bullets: Step 1: difference = 1400 − 500 = **900** cubic centimetres.
Step 2: ratio = 1400 ÷ 500 = **2.8** times.
Step 3: state the trend: cranial capacity **increased** along the human line.

visual.alt: Worked table: 500 and 1400 cubic centimetres, a difference of 900, about 2.8 times larger

slides.narration: Subtract to find how much more, and divide to find how many times more. Our braincase holds about 900 cubic centimetres more, nearly three times as much as that of Australopithecus.

slides.heading: Quick check: brain size
slides.body_md: True or false: Homo erectus had a larger cranial capacity than Homo habilis.
slides.narration: Check the bar chart.

slides.heading: Why walking upright mattered

visual.alt: Flow: upright walking freed the hands for tools and fire, which favoured a larger brain

slides.narration: Walking on two legs freed the hands. Free hands could carry food, make tools and tend a fire. These skills needed planning, so individuals with larger, more capable brains did better and left more children.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Sequence: Australopithecus → Homo habilis → Homo erectus → Neanderthal man → Cro-Magnon man → modern man.
Habilis: tools. Erectus: fully erect, fire. Neanderthal: buried the dead. Cro-Magnon: cave art, chin.
Trends: larger brain, smaller canines and brow ridges, chin appears, less body hair, taller, fully erect.

visual.alt: Summary table of the main trends in human evolution

slides.narration: To recap. Six members, one long story. The brain grew, the face flattened, a chin appeared, and our ancestors stood fully upright, used their hands for tools and fire, and spread across the world.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Learn the **sequence** and one **key fact** for each member.
In comparisons, use **matching points**: posture, cranial capacity, canines, brow ridges, chin, body hair, height.
Cranial capacities are **approximate**; write "about".
Do not say humans evolved **from modern apes**: both share common ancestors.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Know the order and one fact for each. Compare point against point. Write about before every cranial capacity. And remember, humans and apes share ancestors; we did not evolve from the apes alive today.

decks.title: Human Evolution — Part 2: Lamarck and Darwin
goals: Explain Lamarck's theory using the giraffe's neck and human vestigial organs, and state one criticism
Explain the main points of Darwin's theory of natural selection
Explain the change in peppered moth populations during industrialisation

slides.heading: How Does Evolution Happen?
slides.body_md: Part 2 — two famous explanations, and the moth that showed natural selection at work.

visual.alt: Flow: Lamarck's idea of inheritance of acquired characters was replaced by Darwin's natural selection, which was supported by the peppered moth

slides.narration: Living things change over generations. But how? Lamarck gave the first full answer. Darwin gave a better one, and the story of a small moth in industrial England showed his idea working before people’s eyes.

slides.heading: Lamarck's theory

rows: Organs used often grow larger; organs not used shrink
Changes gained during life are passed to the young

visual.alt: Table of Lamarck's two main ideas

slides.narration: Lamarck believed that an animal changes its body by using it, and passes the change to its young. A blacksmith’s strong arms, in his view, would give his children strong arms too.

slides.heading: The giraffe's neck: two explanations
slides.body_md: **Lamarck:** stretching lengthened the neck, and the longer neck was inherited. **Darwin:** necks varied; long-necked giraffes got more food, survived and bred.

slides.heading: Vestigial organs in humans
slides.body_md: **Vestigial organs** are reduced organs with no clear use, though they were useful in our ancestors.

visual.alt: Table of five human vestigial organs and their use in ancestors

slides.narration: Lamarck said these organs shrank because they were not used, and the shrinking was inherited. Today we explain them by natural selection, but they still show that we come from ancestors who used them.

slides.heading: Why Lamarck was rejected

rows: Weismann cut the tails of mice for many generations
Young were always born with normal tails

visual.alt: Table of evidence against Lamarck's theory

slides.narration: Weismann cut the tails off mice, generation after generation, yet every baby had a normal tail. Changes to the body during life do not reach the sex cells, so they are not inherited. Lamarck’s second idea failed the test.

slides.heading: Darwin's theory of natural selection
slides.body_md: **Overproduction → struggle for existence → variation → survival of the fittest → inheritance of useful variations → new species.**

visual.alt: Flow of Darwin's theory: overproduction leads to a struggle for existence; together with variation this leads to survival of the fittest; useful variations are inherited and new species arise over many generations

slides.narration: Darwin noticed that living things produce far more young than can survive. They struggle for food and space. No two are alike. Those with useful differences survive and pass them on. Over many generations this natural selection can produce new species.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: Darwin's giraffe, step by step
slides.body_md: Apply Darwin's points one by one.
bullets: Step 1, **overproduction:** many young giraffes are born.
Step 2, **variation:** their necks differ in length.
Step 3, **struggle and survival:** when low leaves run out, the longest necks reach food; short-necked young starve.
Step 4, **inheritance:** survivors pass on long necks; the average neck lengthens over generations.

visual.alt: Worked table matching Darwin's points to the giraffe

slides.narration: For any example, march through Darwin’s points in order. Too many young, differences among them, a struggle in which some differences help, and inheritance of the helpful ones. That is natural selection.

slides.heading: Quick check: the phrase
slides.narration: Best suited, not strongest.

slides.body_md: Before industry, **light** moths were hidden on pale, lichen-covered bark. When soot blackened the trees, **dark** moths were hidden and light ones were eaten by birds, so the **dark form** became common: **industrial melanism**.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: moth data
slides.body_md: Equal numbers (**100** of each) of marked light and dark moths were released in a sooty wood; **40** dark and **10** light were caught again.
bullets: Step 1: dark recaptured = 40 of 100 = **40 per cent**; light = **10 per cent**.
Step 2: dark survived **4 times** as well as light.
Step 3: link to selection: birds found the light moths more easily. A survey there found **90 per cent** dark moths.

visual.alt: Worked table: of 100 moths of each form, 40 dark and 10 light were recaptured

slides.narration: Turn the counts into percentages so they can be compared. Forty in a hundred dark moths came back, but only ten in a hundred light ones. Dark moths survived 4 times as well, because birds could not see them on the sooty bark.

slides.heading: Lamarck and Darwin compared

rows: Yes, with the help of genetics

visual.alt: Table comparing Lamarck and Darwin

slides.narration: Lamarck said bodies change by use and pass the change on. Darwin said bodies already differ at birth, and nature selects the useful differences. Darwin’s idea, supported by genetics, is the one accepted today.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Lamarck: use and disuse; inheritance of acquired characters (giraffe, vestigial organs).
Weismann's mice showed acquired characters are not inherited.
Darwin: overproduction, struggle, variation, survival of the fittest, inheritance.
Peppered moth: industrial melanism shows natural selection.

visual.alt: Summary table of the key phrase for each theory

slides.narration: To recap. Lamarck thought use changes the body and the change is inherited, but experiments proved him wrong. Darwin showed that nature selects among inborn differences, and the peppered moth let us watch it happen.

bullets: Write **acquired** characters for Lamarck and **inborn variations** for Darwin.
For the moth, mention **soot**, **lichens**, **camouflage**, **birds** and **inheritance**.
"Fittest" means **best suited**, not strongest.
Give **Weismann** as the criticism of Lamarck.

notes.title: Human Evolution — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Human ancestors and how they compare
sections.body_md:
**Sequence:** Australopithecus → Homo habilis → Homo erectus → Neanderthal man → Cro-Magnon man → modern man (*Homo sapiens sapiens*).

| Member | Approx. cranial capacity (cubic cm) | Key features |
|---|---|---|
| Australopithecus | about 500 | Walked on two legs but partly stooped; large canines, heavy brow ridges, no chin, hairy, short |
| Homo habilis | about 700 | "Handy man": first stone tools; brow ridges, no chin |
| Homo erectus | about 1000 | "Upright man": fully erect; used fire; heavy brow ridges, no chin, taller |
| Neanderthal man | about 1450 | Stocky, slightly stooped; heavy brow ridges, receding chin; buried the dead |
| Cro-Magnon man | about 1600 | Tall, fully erect; small brow ridges, prominent chin; cave paintings, fine tools |
| Modern man (Homo sapiens sapiens) | about 1400 | Fully erect; small canines and brow ridges, prominent chin, little body hair; language, farming |

**Trends from Australopithecus to modern man**
- **Posture:** from partly stooped to **fully erect**, with efficient walking on two legs (**bipedalism**).
- **Cranial capacity:** **increases** (about 500 → about 1400 cubic centimetres).
- **Canines:** become **smaller**. **Brow ridges:** become **smaller**. **Chin:** **appears** (Cro-Magnon and modern man).
- **Body hair:** **decreases**. **Height:** **increases**.

Humans did not evolve from today's apes; humans and apes share **common ancestors**.

sections.heading: 2. Lamarck's theory: inheritance of acquired characters
sections.body_md:
Jean-Baptiste **Lamarck** (1809) proposed:
1. **Use and disuse:** organs that are used often become larger and stronger; organs not used become smaller and may disappear.
2. **Inheritance of acquired characters:** changes gained during an organism's life are **passed on** to its young.

**Giraffe:** ancestors with short necks stretched to reach leaves; their necks lengthened a little; the longer necks were inherited, generation after generation.

**Vestigial organs in humans** (reduced, no clear use): vermiform appendix, coccyx (tail bones), ear muscles, nictitating membrane (fold in the eye corner), wisdom teeth. Lamarck explained them by **disuse**.

**Criticism:** **Weismann** cut off the tails of mice for many generations; the young were always born with normal tails. Acquired characters are **not inherited**, because they do not change the genes in the sex cells (other examples: muscles of a body-builder, pierced ears).

key_terms.definition_md: A change gained during an organism's life, not present at birth.
A reduced organ with no clear function, useful in ancestors.

sections.heading: 3. Darwin's theory of natural selection; the peppered moth
sections.body_md:
Charles **Darwin** (*On the Origin of Species*, 1859):
1. **Overproduction:** organisms produce far more young than can survive.
2. **Struggle for existence:** food and space are limited, so there is competition — within a species (intraspecific), between species (interspecific) and with the environment.
3. **Variation:** no two individuals are alike; many differences are inherited.
4. **Survival of the fittest (natural selection):** individuals with useful variations survive and reproduce more.
5. **Inheritance:** useful variations are passed on; over many generations they build up and **new species** arise.

**Giraffe (Darwin):** necks varied at birth; long-necked giraffes reached more food, survived and bred.

**Peppered moth** (*Biston betularia*), England: a **light** and a **dark** form.
- Before industry, tree bark was pale with **lichens**: light moths were camouflaged, dark ones eaten by **birds**; the light form was common.
- In the industrial 1800s, **soot** killed lichens and blackened bark: dark moths were camouflaged and light ones eaten; the dark form became common (**industrial melanism**).
- After **clean-air laws** in the 1900s, bark grew paler and the light form increased again.
The moths did not change colour; birds **selected** among forms that already existed.

key_terms.definition_md: Survival and reproduction of individuals with useful variations.
Increase of dark forms in areas darkened by industrial soot.
Competition for limited resources among the many young produced.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying humans evolved from monkeys or modern apes.
- Giving exact cranial capacities as fixed values (write "about").
- Saying the peppered moths turned dark because of soot (soot changed the bark, not the moths).
- Mixing Lamarck's "acquired characters" with Darwin's "inborn variations".
- Taking "fittest" to mean strongest.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a term, an ancestor, an odd one out **with its category**.
- 2 marks: two differences, or one theory's explanation of an example.
- 3 marks: the points of Darwin's theory, the moth story with camouflage and inheritance, or three trends.

questions.stem_md: Which of these comes earliest in the sequence of human ancestors?
questions.solution_md: The sequence is Australopithecus → Homo habilis → Homo erectus → Neanderthal man → Cro-Magnon man → modern man — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Why was the name "handy man" given to Homo habilis? Because it

options.text_md: made and used simple stone tools
was the first to grow crops

questions.solution_md: Habilis means handy: it shaped stones into simple tools — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The ancestor that walked fully upright and is the first known to have used fire was
questions.solution_md: Homo erectus ("upright man") had a fully erect posture and used fire — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which statement about Neanderthal man is correct?

options.text_md: It had a prominent chin and no brow ridges
It buried its dead and had a brain about as large as ours
It was the first ancestor to walk on two legs
It had a cranial capacity of about 500 cubic centimetres

questions.solution_md: Neanderthals had heavy brow ridges, no chin, a cranial capacity of about 1450 cubic centimetres, and buried their dead — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In a cave, archaeologists find paintings of bison and finely carved bone needles beside skulls that have a chin and a braincase of about 1600 cubic centimetres. The people who left them were most likely

questions.stem_md: Which feature is present in modern humans but absent in Australopithecus?
questions.solution_md: The chin appears only in Cro-Magnon and modern humans; the other three are features of early ancestors — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which trend is seen from Australopithecus to modern humans?

options.text_md: Cranial capacity increases and the brow ridges become smaller

questions.solution_md: Brain size rises, brow ridges and canines shrink, body hair decreases and posture becomes fully erect — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A fossil skull has a low sloping forehead, heavy brow ridges, no chin and a braincase of about 1000 cubic centimetres. Fossil leg bones found with it show a fully upright stance. It most likely belongs to
questions.solution_md: About 1000 cubic centimetres with brow ridges, no chin and an erect posture fits Homo erectus; Australopithecus had about 500, while Cro-Magnon and modern humans have chins — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Australopithecus walked on two legs.

**Reason (R):** Australopithecus had a cranial capacity of only about 500 cubic centimetres.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but a small brain does not explain walking on two legs — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Neanderthal man had a prominent chin.

**Reason (R):** Neanderthal man had heavy brow ridges.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is false: Neanderthals had little or no chin. The reason is true — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Homo erectus had a larger cranial capacity than Homo habilis.
questions.solution_md: True. About 1000 cubic centimetres against about 700.

questions.stem_md: Homo habilis, the first maker of stone tools, is known as the ______ man.
questions.solution_md: Handy man.

questions.stem_md: Give the term: the volume of the braincase of a skull, used to compare the brain size of human ancestors.

answer.model_answer_md: **Cranial capacity.**

questions.solution_md: Cranial capacity.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Prominent chin, Heavy brow ridges, Large canines, Sloping forehead.

answer.model_answer_md: **Prominent chin**; the others are **features of early human ancestors** that were reduced in modern humans.

questions.solution_md: The chin is a modern feature.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: the use of fire was an important step in human evolution.

answer.model_answer_md: Fire gave **warmth and protection** from animals, and **cooked food** was easier to chew and digest.

questions.solution_md: Warmth, safety, cooked food.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these in the order in which they appeared, starting with the earliest: Cro-Magnon man, Homo erectus, Australopithecus, Neanderthal man, Homo habilis. Name the one with the largest cranial capacity.

answer.model_answer_md: **Australopithecus → Homo habilis → Homo erectus → Neanderthal man → Cro-Magnon man.** The largest cranial capacity, about 1600 cubic centimetres, belonged to **Cro-Magnon man**.

questions.solution_md: Correct sequence; Cro-Magnon.

questions.stem_md: Give two differences between Homo habilis and Homo erectus.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Homo habilis had a smaller brain (about **700** cubic centimetres); Homo erectus a larger one (about **1000**).
2. Homo habilis made **simple stone tools**; Homo erectus walked **fully upright** and used **fire**.

questions.solution_md: Brain size; posture and fire.

questions.stem_md: Compare Australopithecus with modern humans in cranial capacity, brow ridges and chin.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Feature | Australopithecus | Modern human |
|---|---|---|
| Cranial capacity | About **500** cubic centimetres | About **1400** cubic centimetres |
| Brow ridges | **Heavy, prominent** | **Small** |
| Chin | **Absent** | **Prominent** |

questions.solution_md: Three features compared.

questions.stem_md: According to Lamarck, the giraffe's long neck developed because

options.text_md: giraffes born with longer necks survived droughts and bred more
a single sudden change produced a long neck in one generation
generations of giraffes stretched their necks to reach leaves and passed on the longer necks
giraffes ate a special leaf that lengthened the neck

questions.solution_md: Lamarck believed that use lengthened the neck and that this acquired change was inherited — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which human organ is reduced and has no clear use today, although it was useful to our ancestors?
questions.solution_md: The appendix is reduced and has no clear digestive role in humans — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Weismann cut off the tails of mice over many generations, yet every new generation was born with normal tails. This shows that

options.text_md: characters acquired during life are not inherited
use and disuse change the body
mice can grow back lost tails

questions.solution_md: Cutting the tail changed only the body, not the sex cells, so the change was not passed on — option (a).

questions.stem_md: How would a supporter of Lamarck explain the small size of the human vermiform appendix?

options.text_md: Individuals with small appendixes survived better and bred more
It shrank through disuse over many generations, and the shrinking was inherited
A sudden mutation removed most of it
It is still used to digest cellulose

questions.solution_md: Lamarck held that organs not used become smaller and that this change is inherited — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A wrestler's children are not born with large muscles.

**Reason (R):** Characters acquired during a lifetime do not change the genes in the sex cells.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and since exercise does not alter the genes passed on in sperm or egg, the muscles are not inherited — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Lamarck's theory is also called the theory of inheritance of acquired characters.
questions.solution_md: True. Lamarck proposed that changes acquired by use or disuse are passed on.

questions.stem_md: Organs that are reduced and have no clear function, though they were useful in our ancestors, are called ______ organs.
questions.solution_md: Vestigial organs.

questions.stem_md: Give the term: Lamarck's idea that organs used often grow larger and stronger, while those not used become smaller.

answer.model_answer_md: **Use and disuse of organs.**

questions.solution_md: Use and disuse.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Vermiform appendix, Wisdom teeth, Muscles that move the ear, Thumb.

answer.model_answer_md: **Thumb**; the others are **vestigial organs** in humans.

questions.solution_md: The thumb is fully functional.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: Lamarck's theory was not accepted.

answer.model_answer_md: Experiments such as **Weismann's** showed that **acquired characters are not inherited**; only changes in the **genes of the sex cells** are passed on.

questions.solution_md: Acquired characters not inherited.

questions.stem_md: State the two main ideas of Lamarck's theory.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Use and disuse:** organs that are used a lot grow larger and stronger; those not used shrink and may disappear.
2. **Inheritance of acquired characters:** changes gained in this way during life are **passed on** to the young.

questions.solution_md: Use and disuse; inheritance of acquired characters.

questions.stem_md: Name two vestigial organs in humans, and state how Lamarck explained such organs.

answer.model_answer_md: Examples: the **vermiform appendix** and the **tail bones (coccyx)**; also wisdom teeth and ear muscles. Lamarck said they became small through **disuse**, and the reduced size was **inherited** by later generations.

questions.solution_md: Two organs; disuse.

questions.stem_md: "Survival of the fittest" means that

options.text_md: the strongest animals always win fights
all individuals of a species survive equally
individuals with variations best suited to their surroundings survive and reproduce more
organisms change their bodies on purpose to suit their needs

questions.solution_md: Fitness means being better suited to the environment, which leads to more surviving offspring — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A pair of rabbits could in theory have millions of descendants in a few years, yet the number of rabbits in a meadow stays about the same. Darwin called the first fact
questions.solution_md: Living things produce far more young than can survive — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Two male deer fighting for the same territory is an example of
questions.solution_md: Both deer belong to the same species and compete for the same resource — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Before industrial pollution in England, the light form of the peppered moth was more common because

options.text_md: dark moths could not fly in clean air
light moths laid more eggs in clean air
it was hidden on pale, lichen-covered tree trunks and escaped birds
birds preferred to eat light moths

questions.solution_md: Camouflage on pale bark protected the light form from birds — option (c).

questions.stem_md: After clean-air laws reduced soot, the light form of the peppered moth became common again in industrial areas. This supports

options.text_md: Lamarck's theory, because the moths chose to change colour
the idea that soot directly bleached the moths
the inheritance of characters acquired by use
natural selection, because the cleaner bark changed which form was better hidden

questions.solution_md: As bark grew paler, birds again picked off the dark moths, so selection favoured the light form — option (d).

questions.stem_md: According to Darwin, giraffes came to have long necks because

options.text_md: each giraffe stretched its neck and passed on the stretch
giraffes that happened to be born with longer necks got more food, survived and passed on the trait
giraffes needed long necks and so grew them
the climate directly lengthened their necks

questions.solution_md: Natural variation plus selection by food supply, not use, explains the long neck — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The dark form of the peppered moth became common because soot turned light moths black.

**Reason (R):** Birds ate more of the moths that stood out against the tree bark.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is false: soot did not change the colour of moths; the dark form was already present and survived better. The reason is true — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Darwin's theory of evolution is called the theory of natural selection.

**Reason (R):** Darwin collected many of his observations during a long voyage on the ship HMS Beagle.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but the voyage does not explain why the theory has that name — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Overproduction of young leads to a struggle for existence.

**Reason (R):** Food, space and other resources are limited.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and because resources are limited, the many young must compete for them — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? According to Darwin, no two individuals of a species are exactly alike.
questions.solution_md: True. These small differences, or variations, are the raw material for natural selection.

questions.stem_md: The idea that only the best-suited individuals survive to reproduce is summed up as "survival of the ______".
questions.solution_md: Survival of the fittest.

questions.stem_md: Give the term: the rise in the number of dark-coloured forms of a species in areas darkened by industrial soot.

answer.model_answer_md: **Industrial melanism.**

questions.solution_md: Industrial melanism.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Overproduction, Struggle for existence, Variation, Use and disuse.

answer.model_answer_md: **Use and disuse**; the others are **points of Darwin's theory of natural selection**.

questions.solution_md: Use and disuse is Lamarck's idea.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: dark peppered moths survived better than light ones in soot-covered woods.

answer.model_answer_md: Dark moths were **camouflaged** on the dark bark, so **birds could not easily see** and eat them.

questions.solution_md: Camouflage from birds.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between Lamarck's and Darwin's explanations of the giraffe's long neck.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Lamarck:** giraffes **stretched** their necks to reach leaves, the necks lengthened by use, and this **acquired** length was passed on.
**Darwin:** giraffes were **born** with necks of different lengths; those with longer necks got more food, **survived** and passed on the trait.

questions.solution_md: Use and inheritance vs variation and selection.

questions.stem_md: Each year far more caterpillars hatch on a farmer's cabbages than ever become butterflies, yet the number of butterflies stays about the same. Using this example, explain in three points how Darwin's natural selection works.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Overproduction:** the butterflies lay far more eggs than can ever survive.
2. **Struggle for existence:** the caterpillars compete for limited cabbage leaves and are eaten by birds, so most die.
3. **Variation and survival of the fittest:** the caterpillars differ, for example in colour; the best-hidden survive, breed and **pass on** that trait, so it becomes common over generations.

questions.solution_md: Overproduction, struggle, variation, survival of the fittest, inheritance.

marking_scheme.step: Variation, survival of the fittest and inheritance

questions.stem_md: In a survey in a soot-darkened wood, 180 of the 200 peppered moths found were of the dark form. What percentage were dark?
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{180}{200} \times 100 = 90$ per cent.

questions.stem_md:
Select the correct terms to fill in the blanks: [Australopithecus, Homo habilis, Homo erectus, Neanderthal, Cro-Magnon, chin, fire, cave paintings]

The earliest ancestor in the human line was (a) ______, which walked on two legs but had a small brain. (b) ______ was the first to make stone tools. (c) ______ walked fully upright and was the first to use (d) ______. Cro-Magnon man is famous for its (e) ______.

questions.passage_md: Students studied a model of an experiment on the peppered moth. Equal numbers of light and dark moths (100 of each) were marked and released in a soot-darkened wood. A few days later, 40 dark and 10 light marked moths were caught again; the rest had mostly been eaten by birds. A survey in a clean wood with lichen-covered trees found 30 dark and 170 light moths.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The **dark form.**

**(b)** 4

**(c)** 15 %

**(d)** Soot killed the pale lichens and **blackened the tree bark**. On dark bark, the dark moths were **camouflaged**, while light moths stood out and were **eaten by birds**. More dark moths **survived and bred**, passing on their colour, so over many generations the dark form became **common**.

**(e)** (i) As soot fell, the bark grew **paler** again, so the **light form** was now better hidden and survived more. The change came from **birds selecting** among moths that were **already different** in colour, not from moths changing their colour by effort or use, as Lamarck would suggest. This is **natural selection**.

**OR** (ii) **Industrial melanism.** It shows (1) **variation**: light and dark forms exist; (2) **struggle for existence**: moths must escape birds; (3) **survival of the fittest**: the better-hidden form survives and breeds, so it becomes common.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Dark form.

**(b)** 40 ÷ 10 = 4 times.

**(c)** Total $= 30 + 170 = 200$; dark $= \dfrac{30}{200} \times 100 = 15$ per cent.

**(d)** Camouflage, predation, survival, inheritance.

**(e)** (i) Selection of existing variants.

(ii) Industrial melanism; variation, struggle, survival.

questions.passage_md: The figure compares two explanations of how the giraffe came to have a long neck. The top row follows one scientist's idea and the bottom row another's.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Lamarck's** theory.

**(b)** Giraffes **stretched** their necks to reach leaves high up. By this constant **use** their necks grew a little longer, and the **acquired** longer neck was passed on to their young. Over many generations the neck became very long.

**(c)** Giraffes are **born** with necks of different lengths (**variation**). When food is only high up, those with **longer necks** get more food and **survive**, while short-necked ones starve. The survivors **breed** and pass on long necks, so the trait becomes common.

**(d)** **Weismann** cut off the **tails of mice** and bred them, repeating this for **many generations**. Every new generation was still born with **normal tails**. He concluded that changes made to the body during life (**acquired characters**) are **not inherited**; only what is carried in the sex cells is passed on.

**(e)** (i) The **vermiform appendix** and the **coccyx** (tail bones). Darwin would say that once they were no longer useful, **natural selection** no longer kept them large, so over many generations smaller forms were not at a disadvantage and became common.

**OR** (ii) 1. The **children of a body-builder** are not born with large muscles.
2. A person who loses a finger in an accident has **children with normal hands**; likewise, children of parents with pierced ears are born without holes.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Lamarck.

**(b)** Use and inheritance of acquired characters.

**(c)** Variation and natural selection.

**(d)** Weismann's mice.

**(e)** (i) Two organs; selection, not use.

(ii) Two everyday examples.
